questions.stem: The arid soils of the Thar Desert in Rajasthan are paradoxically notable for containing unusually high levels of which nutrient, despite being severely deficient in nitrogen and organic matter?

options.option_text: Calcium — abundant due to heavy leaching in alluvial zones
Soluble phosphates — unusually high in Thar desert arid soils
Potassium — leached from alluvial soils but retained in arid zones
Manganese — concentrated through evaporation in hot dry zones

questions.explanation: Arid/desert soils of the Thar region are characterised by low humus and nitrogen but are notable for relatively high soluble phosphate content. This is because the dry conditions prevent leaching of phosphates. Calcium is NOT the defining distinguishing nutrient; phosphate content is the textbook differentiator for Indian arid soils.

questions.stem: The low-lying wetlands of the Kuttanad region in Kerala contain a distinctive dark soil locally called 'Kari', used for rice cultivation below sea level. 'Kari' belongs to which broader Indian soil category?

options.option_text: Alluvial soils deposited by river sediment over floodplains
Laterite soils formed through intense tropical chemical leaching
Peaty and marshy soils rich in decomposed organic matter
Saline soils degraded by repeated tidal seawater intrusion

questions.explanation: Kari soils of Kuttanad (Kerala) are a classic example of peaty and marshy soils — formed in water-logged conditions through accumulation of partially decomposed organic matter (peat). They are highly acidic. Option D (saline) is the most tempting distractor because Kuttanad is coastal, but the defining characteristic is organic-peat accumulation, not salt loading.

questions.stem: In irrigated canal command areas of the Indo-Gangetic Plains, productive soils progressively turn saline and are locally called 'Reh', 'Usar' or 'Kallar'. Which process is the PRIMARY driver of this degradation?

options.option_text: Intense leaching that strips base cations down to deeper horizons
Capillary rise of saline groundwater and salt deposition on evaporation
Wind-borne deposition of salt particles from coastal tidal flats
Acidification by monsoon waterlogging in low-lying depressions

questions.explanation: Secondary salinisation in canal-irrigated tracts occurs when irrigation raises the shallow water table. Saline groundwater then moves upward by capillary action and deposits salts at the surface as water evaporates — forming Usar/Reh/Kallar. Option A (leaching) is the opposite process and actually reduces salinity. Coastal wind-salt deposition is negligible in the deep Gangetic plains.

questions.stem: The self-ploughing property of Black Cotton (Regur) soil — deep vertical cracking when dry and swelling shut when wet — is directly caused by the dominance of which clay mineral in its composition?

options.option_text: Montmorillonite — a 2:1 lattice clay with very high water absorption
Kaolinite — a 1:1 lattice clay mineral with low shrink-swell capacity
Illite — a potassium-rich clay mineral with moderate plasticity
Chlorite — an iron-magnesium clay with a rigid, non-expanding lattice

questions.explanation: Montmorillonite (smectite group), a 2:1 expanding lattice clay, absorbs large amounts of water between its crystal layers causing the soil to swell; on drying it contracts sharply, forming the characteristic gilgai cracks. Kaolinite (Option B) is the most common distractor but it is a non-expanding 1:1 clay found in laterite soils — it does NOT cause shrink-swell behaviour.

questions.stem: Mountain soils found on upper Himalayan slopes above approximately 3,000 metres altitude are agronomically challenging primarily because they are characterised as?

options.option_text: Neutral to alkaline, deep-profile soils rich in calcium carbonate
Well-structured, deep soils with high levels of decomposed humus
Alkaline, sandy-textured soils with high concentrations of soluble salts
Acidic, shallow, and deficient in potash and phosphorus content

questions.explanation: Mountain soils above 3,000 m are thin and acidic due to cold, wet conditions that restrict decomposition, and they are notably deficient in potash and phosphorus. Option B is the tempting distractor — lower Himalayan forested slopes do have better humus; but higher altitude soils are shallow, skeletal, and nutrient-poor. Alkalinity (Options A/C) is the opposite of observed conditions.

questions.stem: Under the USDA Soil Taxonomy system — formally adopted by ICAR for classifying Indian soils — the black cotton soils of the Deccan Trap region are placed under which soil order, defined by vertic properties and gilgai microrelief?

options.option_text: Alfisols — moderately leached soils with clay-enriched B horizon
Inceptisols — young soils with weakly differentiated soil horizons
Vertisols — dark, smectite-rich shrink-swell clays with gilgai relief
Mollisols — humus-rich, soft, dark epipedon soils of grasslands

questions.explanation: Vertisols (from Latin 'verto' = to turn) are defined by >30% smectite (montmorillonite) clay, slickensides, gilgai microrelief, and vertic crack formation — all hallmarks of Deccan's black cotton soils. Mollisols (Option D) is the most dangerous distractor because they are also dark, organic-rich soils, but Mollisols form in humid grasslands; Vertisols form in seasonally dry sub-humid climates and are defined by the shrink-swell, not organic matter.

questions.stem: ICAR-NBSS&LUP soil health surveys consistently identify one micronutrient as deficient in over 50% of India's agricultural soils — especially in the alluvial plains — making it the most widespread micronutrient deficiency in Indian agriculture. Which element is this?

options.option_text: Boron — critical for cell wall integrity and pollen tube germination
Zinc — vital for enzyme activation, auxin synthesis, and grain filling
Manganese — essential for photosystem II and nitrogen fixation enzymes
Copper — required for lignin biosynthesis and electron transport chains

questions.explanation: Zinc deficiency is documented as the most widespread micronutrient deficiency in Indian soils — ICAR surveys show it affects 48–52% of surveyed soils, especially calcareous alluvial soils of the IGP where high pH immobilises zinc. It causes khaira disease in paddy and white bud in maize. Boron (Option A) is second most widespread but still far behind zinc; manganese deficiency is rare in India's neutral-alkaline soils.
